
.github/workflows/release.yml:26 — the attachment is disabled:

```yaml
        # extra_files: LICENSE README.md
```

so published release archives carry neither the license nor the README.

README.md:191-197 solicits contributions ("Fork the repository … Open a Pull Request") and README.md:30 advertises `go install github.com/ivuorinen/pinboard-checker@latest`, both of which presume rights the repository has not granted.

Dependency licenses are, by contrast, unproblematic — `godotenv` (MIT), `progressbar/v3` (MIT), `golang.org/x/net` (BSD-3-Clause), `colorstring` (MIT), `uniseg` (MIT), and `golang.org/x/sys`/`x/term` (BSD-3-Clause) are all permissive with no copyleft contamination, and all are compatible with any license the project might choose.</evidence>
<parameter name="impact">Users and distributors have no legal permission to use the tool despite it being published for that purpose, and contributors have no stated terms under which their contributions are accepted. Release archives ship without any license text, so even a downstream user acting in good faith has nothing to comply with. Package indexes and license scanners will report the module as unlicensed.</impact>
<parameter name="fix">Add a `LICENSE` file at the repository root with the intended terms. MIT matches the permissive posture of every dependency and the "fork it" contribution guidance:

```
MIT License

Copyright (c) 2026 Ismo Vuorinen

Permission is hereby granted, free of charge, to any person obtaining a copy
...
```

Then enable the release attachment, .github/workflows/release.yml:26:

```yaml
        extra_files: LICENSE README.md
```

and name the license explicitly in `README.md` rather than deferring to the file:

```markdown
## License

MIT — see [LICENSE](LICENSE).
```

Adding the SPDX identifier to the README badge area or to `go.mod` metadata is optional but makes the license machine-readable for scanners.</fix>
</invoke>

## Impact

## Fix

## Resolution
Added an MIT LICENSE, "Copyright (c) 2024 Ismo Vuorinen" (first commit year). MIT was chosen to match the owner's convention — 70 of 82 licensed repos on the account are MIT — and is compatible with every dependency (all MIT or BSD-3-Clause). README's License section now names MIT and links the file instead of pointing at a file that did not exist. Uncommented extra_files in release.yml so LICENSE and README ship with the release archives. Confirm the license choice if MIT is not intended.

## Problem

Three concrete disagreements between `README.md` and the implementation, each in a section a user would rely on to decide how to run the tool.

1. The Options list omits `-workers`, a flag that exists, defaults to 10, and can deadlock the process at 0.
2. The Troubleshooting section describes timeout behaviour the program does not have.
3. Neither the Auto-Tagging feature description nor the How It Works walkthrough mentions that `.autoTagged` begins with a period and therefore triggers Pinboard's private-tag semantics.</problem>
<parameter name="evidence">**1. Missing flag.** README.md:114-121 lists six flags:

```markdown
- `-token string`: Pinboard API token ...
- `-dry-run`: ...
- `-verbose`: ...
- `-ci`: ...
- `-skip-titles`: ...
- `-skip-auto-tags`: ...
```

main.go:77 defines a seventh:

```go
workers := flag.Int("workers", 10, "Number of concurrent workers for parallel processing")
```

README.md:14 alludes to it ("configurable, default 10 workers") without naming the flag, so a reader cannot discover the spelling.

**2. Timeouts.** README.md:219-222:

```markdown
### Timeouts

Some URLs may timeout if the target server is slow to respond. These will be marked
as errors and can be deleted or skipped based on your preferences.
```

No client in the program sets a `Timeout` — all nine request sites use `http.DefaultClient`, whose timeout is zero (filed separately). There is no timeout to be marked as an error, and no preference exists that selects between deleting and skipping; every error becomes `ActionDelete` unconditionally (main.go:126-135).

**3. Private tags.** README.md:20:

```markdown
- **Auto-Tagging**: Adds up to 10 suggested tags (from Pinboard API) for untagged bookmarks
```

README.md:134-135:

```markdown
     - Gets up to 10 tags from Pinboard's suggestion API
     - Always adds `.autoTagged` marker tag
```

Pinboard API documentation, Data Types:

> `tag` — up to 255 characters. May not contain commas or whitespace. Please be aware that tags beginning with a period are treated as private and trigger special private tag semantics.

The count is also wrong: `collectTagsFromSuggestions` applies its cap before appending the marker, so the result is 11 tags, and `TestGetSuggestedTags_MaxTenTags` (main_test.go:274) asserts exactly that.</evidence>
<parameter name="impact">A user reading the Options list has no way to learn `-workers` exists or that `-workers 0` hangs. A user hitting a hung run consults the Troubleshooting section and is told the tool handles timeouts, so they wait rather than investigate. A user adopting auto-tagging is not told the tool applies a Pinboard private tag to every bookmark it touches, which changes how those bookmarks behave on the service.</impact>
<parameter name="fix">1. Add the flag to README.md:114-121:

```markdown
- `-workers int`: Number of concurrent workers for parallel processing (default: 10, minimum: 1)
```

## Problem

Three separate maintainability defects, grouped because each is a one-line fix.

1. `expandAndCheckURL` names its parameter `url`, shadowing the imported `net/url` package for the whole function body. It compiles only because that function happens never to need the package — any future line calling `url.Parse` there fails to compile with a confusing error.
2. `Statistics.TotalErrors` is incremented but never read or printed: dead state that looks like a reported metric.
3. `golangci-lint` reports 13 `goconst` issues, all in test files, none addressed.</problem>
<parameter name="evidence">**1. Package shadowing.** main.go:587 — the parameter takes the package's name:

```go
func expandAndCheckURL(url string, verbose bool) (string, error) {
```

while main.go:9 imports it:

```go
	"net/url"
```

Every sibling function avoids the collision by naming the parameter `urlString` or `urlStr` — main.go:473, :521, :618, :639, :674 — so this is a single inconsistent site, not a house convention:

```go
func getPageTitle(urlString string) (string, error)
func validateURLAccessibility(urlString, context string) error
func fixParenthesesSuffix(urlString string, verbose bool) (string, error)
func urlRedirects(urlString string, verbose bool) (string, error)
```

`predeclared` is enabled (.golangci.yml:72) but only covers predeclared identifiers, not imported package names; `revive`'s `import-shadowing` rule, which would catch this, is not among the rules configured at .golangci.yml:~140.

**2. Dead field.** statistics.go:50-51:

```go
	// Errors
	TotalErrors int
```

Its only write is statistics.go:74:

```go
	case ActionDelete:
		s.ActionDelete++
		s.TotalErrors++
```

It appears in none of the eight `print*` methods (statistics.go:145-315) and in no test. `unused` (.golangci.yml:39) does not flag it because struct fields written but never read are outside its analysis.


## Problem

Every one of the nine HTTP call sites repeats the same five-line deferred body-close block. A constant, `ErrClosingBodyMsg`, exists for the message — and only five of the nine sites use it. The other four re-inline the identical string literal, so the constant does not actually centralise anything.

All nine write to stdout rather than stderr, mixing a diagnostic into the program's normal output.</problem>
<parameter name="evidence">The constant, main.go:20-23:

```go
const (
	ErrClosingBodyMsg = "Error closing response body: %v\n"
	tokenName         = "PINBOARD_API_TOKEN" //nolint:gosec // Not a credential, just the env var name
)
```

Split usage — five sites use it, five re-inline it:

```
$ grep -n 'ErrClosingBodyMsg' main.go
21:	ErrClosingBodyMsg = "Error closing response body: %v\n"
625:			fmt.Printf(ErrClosingBodyMsg, closeErr)
656:			fmt.Printf(ErrClosingBodyMsg, closeErr)
687:			fmt.Printf(ErrClosingBodyMsg, closeErr)
754:			fmt.Printf(ErrClosingBodyMsg, closeErr)
773:			fmt.Printf(ErrClosingBodyMsg, closeErr)

$ grep -n 'Error closing response body' main.go
21:	ErrClosingBodyMsg = "Error closing response body: %v\n"
389:			fmt.Printf("Error closing response body: %v\n", err)
436:			fmt.Printf("Error closing response body: %v\n", err)
461:			fmt.Printf("Error closing response body: %v\n", err)
480:			fmt.Printf("Error closing response body: %v\n", err)
535:			fmt.Printf("Error closing response body: %v\n", err)
```

The two variants also differ in the error variable they bind — `err` at 387-391, shadowing the enclosing `err`, versus `closeErr` at 623-627:

```go
	defer func() {
		if err := resp.Body.Close(); err != nil {
			fmt.Printf("Error closing response body: %v\n", err)
		}
	}()
```

```go
	defer func() {
		if closeErr := resp.Body.Close(); closeErr != nil {
			fmt.Printf(ErrClosingBodyMsg, closeErr)
		}
	}()
```

`goconst` (.golangci.yml:45) does not catch the split because it excludes strings already declared as constants, and `dupl` (.golangci.yml:44) does not fire on five-line blocks at its default threshold.

`ErrClosingBodyMsg` is also misnamed for what it is: the `Err` prefix is Go's convention for an `error` value, not a format string.</evidence>
<parameter name="impact">Changing the message, its destination, or the decision to log it at all requires nine edits, and the four inlined copies will be missed by anyone who greps for the constant. The mixed `err`/`closeErr` binding means half the sites shadow the function's own `err` inside the defer, which is the shape that silently swallows a named return value if one is ever added. Writing the diagnostic to stdout means it interleaves with the statistics report and, under `-ci`, with whatever consumes the tool's output.</impact>
<parameter name="fix">Replace all nine blocks with one helper:

```go
// closeBody closes an HTTP response body and reports a close failure to stderr.
// Close errors are diagnostic only — the response has already been read — so
// they must not reach stdout, where they would interleave with the statistics
// report that callers parse.
func closeBody(body io.Closer) {
	if err := body.Close(); err != nil {
		fmt.Fprintf(os.Stderr, "Error closing response body: %v\n", err)
	}
}
```

and at each call site:

```go
defer closeBody(resp.Body)
```

Then delete `ErrClosingBodyMsg` — the message lives in the helper and needs no exported constant. If a constant is kept for other reasons, rename it away from the `Err` prefix (e.g. `msgClosingBody`), which Go reserves for `error` values.

This removes 36 lines and makes the stdout/stderr decision a single edit. `bodyclose` (.golangci.yml:43) continues to verify every response is closed, so the refactor stays checked.</fix>
</invoke>

## Evidence

## Impact

## Fix

## Resolution
All nine defer blocks replaced with `defer closeBody(resp.Body)`. closeBody writes to stderr rather than stdout, so a close diagnostic no longer interleaves with the statistics report. The ErrClosingBodyMsg constant was deleted along with its four inlined duplicates, removing both the split usage and the misleading Err prefix on what was a format string. bodyclose remains enabled and reports no unclosed bodies.
title: The body-close defer block is duplicated nine times and half the sites ignore the constant defined for it

## Problem

The working tree on `feat/upgrades` modifies `go.mod` to drop the `toolchain go1.26.6` directive and rewrite the language version from `go 1.25.0` to `go 1.25.6`. Commit `a1781d6` is titled "chore(deps): update go toolchain directive (1.26.5 → 1.26.6) [security]" — this uncommitted edit undoes it.

Without a `toolchain` line, the build uses whatever toolchain the developer or runner happens to have. The change also silently reduces the module's minimum-Go floor to a patch-pinned `1.25.6`.

The same working tree also deletes `.envrc` and the two `.serena/` files, and drops 66 lines from `go.sum`, none of it committed.</problem>
<parameter name="evidence">Working-tree diff:

```diff
--- i/go.mod
+++ w/go.mod
@@ -1,8 +1,6 @@
 module github.com/ivuorinen/pinboard-checker
 
-go 1.25.0
-
-toolchain go1.26.6
+go 1.25.6
```

The commit being reverted, from `git log`:

```
a1781d6 chore(deps): update go toolchain directive (1.26.5 → 1.26.6) [security]
```

Full working-tree state:

```
$ git status --short
 D .envrc
 D .serena/.gitignore
 D .serena/project.yml
 M go.mod
 M go.sum
 
$ git diff --stat
 .envrc              |  1 -
 .serena/.gitignore  |  1 -
 .serena/project.yml | 71 -----------------------------------------------------
 go.mod              |  4 +--
 go.sum              | 66 -------------------------------------------------
 5 files changed, 1 insertion(+), 142 deletions(-)
```

The CI workflow pins a third, unrelated version — .github/workflows/go.yml:22:

```yaml
        go-version: '1.26'
```

and `.golangci.yml:12` a fourth:

```yaml
  go: "1.25"
```

and README.md:177 a fifth phrasing:

```markdown
- Go 1.25 or later
```

Local toolchain in use is `go1.25.6`, so the modified `go.mod` builds cleanly here and would not surface the drift — `go build ./...` and `go vet ./...` both pass, and `gofmt -l` is empty.</evidence>
<parameter name="impact">Committing this branch as-is silently reverts a security-motivated toolchain pin, so builds fall back to whatever Go version is installed rather than the vetted 1.26.6. Because the reverted commit is titled `[security]`, the regression is likely to be attributed to Renovate rather than to a manual edit. The five disagreeing version declarations mean no single source of truth exists for what this project targets, and CI (1.26) does not build with the same toolchain the module asks for.</impact>
<parameter name="fix">Restore the directive before committing:

```
go 1.25.0

toolchain go1.26.6
```

`go 1.25.0` is the correct form for a language-version floor — patch-pinning it to `1.25.6` narrows the set of toolchains that will build the module for no benefit, since the `toolchain` line already selects the build toolchain.

If the deletion was deliberate, say so in the commit message and note that it reverts `a1781d6`; a silent revert of a `[security]`-tagged change should not reach `main` unexplained.

Collapse the version drift to one source: set `go-version-file: go.mod` in `.github/workflows/go.yml` (replacing `'1.26'`), drop `run.go` from `.golangci.yml` so golangci-lint reads `go.mod`, and correct README.md:177 to match.

Decide separately on the deleted `.envrc` and `.serena/` files. If tooling files should not be tracked, add them to `.gitignore` in the same commit so they stay untracked rather than reappearing as deletions in every future `git status`.</fix>
</invoke>

## Evidence

## Impact

## Fix

## Resolution
Not a defect: the owner confirmed the toolchain directive was deliberately replaced by setting the go directive in go.mod directly, so go.mod is left as-is. The finding read a deliberate change as an accidental revert of a1781d6. One factual note for the record, which does not reopen the finding: the working tree's `go 1.25.6` is a lower version than the removed `toolchain go1.26.6`, so builds now select 1.25.6 rather than the newer toolchain that commit pinned. The related version-drift half of this finding was addressed separately — CI and .golangci.yml now both follow go.mod instead of carrying their own pins, and README states "Go 1.25.6 or later (see go.mod)".

## Problem

`pinboardGet` builds a URL carrying `auth_token` and wraps any transport failure with `%w`. The wrapped value is a `*url.Error`, whose `Error()` renders the **full request URL including the query string**. The token therefore appears in the error text, which `run` prints to stderr on a failed fetch.

The function's own docstring asserts the opposite: "Errors never include the built URL, which carries the auth token." Naming only `path` in the format string does not help, because the token arrives through the wrapped error rather than the format arguments.

This reintroduces the exact exposure that `audit-7a71e676` (the `-h` flag default) was filed and fixed for.</problem>
<parameter name="evidence">main.go:301-312:

```go
// Errors never include the built URL, which carries the auth token.
func pinboardGet(path string, params url.Values, apiToken string) (*http.Response, error) {
	params.Set("auth_token", apiToken)
	params.Set("format", "json")
	apiURL := pinboardAPIEndpoint + path + "?" + params.Encode()

	for attempt := range maxRateLimitRetries {
		waitForRateLimit()

		resp, err := httpClient.Get(apiURL)
		if err != nil {
			return nil, fmt.Errorf("pinboard %s request failed: %w", path, err)
		}
```

Reproduced on Go 1.26.6 with the same wrapping and a placeholder token:

```
wrapped error: pinboard /posts/all request failed: Get
"http://127.0.0.1:43323/posts/all?auth_token=ivuorinen%3ASUPERSECRETTOKEN&format=json":
dial tcp 127.0.0.1:43323: connect: connection refused
LEAK CONFIRMED: the token appears in the error text
```

`url.Error.Error()` is `fmt.Sprintf("%s %q: %s", e.Op, e.URL, e.Err)` — the URL is unconditional.

The error reaches stderr in main.go:230-233:

```go
	if err != nil {
		fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, "Error fetching bookmarks:", err)

		return 1
	}
```

Every DNS failure, refused connection, and timeout against `api.pinboard.in` therefore prints the token. README.md documents `-ci` for CI/CD pipelines, where stderr is archived — the same log-capture path that made the `-h` default a High finding.

`unshortenBitlyImpl` is unaffected: its token travels in an `Authorization` header, not the URL. `unshortenIsGdImpl` sends no credential.</evidence>
<parameter name="impact">A transient network failure — the most routine error this program can hit — writes the full `username:TOKEN` to stderr and into any CI job log. The token grants complete read/write access to the account. Because the failure is transient and the run exits 1, the operator is likely to re-run and archive the log rather than treat it as a credential incident.</impact>
<parameter name="fix">Strip the URL before wrapping. Unwrap the `*url.Error` and re-wrap with only its operation and cause:

```go
// sanitizeTransportError removes the request URL from a transport error.
// url.Error renders the full URL, and every Pinboard URL carries auth_token in
// its query string, so wrapping the raw error printed the credential to stderr.
func sanitizeTransportError(path string, err error) error {
	var urlErr *url.Error
	if errors.As(err, &urlErr) {
		return fmt.Errorf("pinboard %s request failed: %s: %w", path, urlErr.Op, urlErr.Err)
	}

	return fmt.Errorf("pinboard %s request failed: %w", path, err)
}
```

and call it at main.go:311. `urlErr.Err` is the underlying cause (`connect: connection refused`, `context deadline exceeded`) and carries no URL.

Add a regression test that points `pinboardAPIEndpoint` at a closed port, calls `getBookmarks` with a recognisable token, and asserts the token is absent from `err.Error()`. That test is what makes the docstring's claim true rather than aspirational.

Audit every other site that could wrap a URL-bearing error the same way; `unshortenIsGdImpl` at main.go:1191 builds a URL with no secret, so it is safe, but the same guard is worth applying if a credential is ever added there.</fix>
</invoke>

## Evidence

## Impact

## Fix

## Resolution
Added sanitizeTransportError, which unwraps *url.Error via errors.As and re-wraps with only the operation and the underlying cause, dropping the URL that carried auth_token. pinboardGet now uses it for every transport failure, so the docstring's guarantee is real rather than aspirational. Regression guards: TestPinboardGet_TransportErrorHidesToken and TestUpdateBookmark_TransportErrorHidesToken point the endpoint at a closed port with a recognisable token and assert it is absent from err.Error() while the endpoint path survives.
title: pinboardGet leaks the API token in transport errors, contradicting its own docstring

## Problem

`widenRateLimit` doubles `rateLimitInterval` on every 429 and resets the ticker, but nothing ever narrows it again. The interval is package state that only grows for the lifetime of the process.

Pinboard's documentation asks clients to "keep doubling the interval between requests **until you stop receiving errors**" — the doubling is correct, the absence of any recovery is not.</problem>
<parameter name="evidence">main.go:285-292:

```go
func widenRateLimit() time.Duration {
	rateLimiterMux.Lock()
	defer rateLimiterMux.Unlock()
	rateLimitInterval *= 2
	rateLimiter.Reset(rateLimitInterval)

	return rateLimitInterval
}
```

There is no counterpart. `grep -n 'rateLimitInterval' main.go` shows assignment only at the declaration (main.go:154, `= defaultRateLimit`) and inside `widenRateLimit`.

The doubling is per-retry, not per-call, so a single throttled request can widen the interval four times in one `pinboardGet` invocation (main.go:306-324, `maxRateLimitRetries = 5`):

```
3s → 6s → 12s → 24s → 48s
```

Every subsequent Pinboard call in the run — the title fetches, the tag fetches, and every write in phase two — then waits 48 seconds at main.go:276-280, whether or not Pinboard is still throttling.

Concrete failure: an account of 500 untagged bookmarks that hits one burst of 429s early in phase one goes from 500 × 3s ≈ 25 minutes to 500 × 48s ≈ 6.7 hours, with no output explaining why. Because `-timeout` bounds individual requests and not the run, nothing interrupts it.</evidence>
<parameter name="impact">A single transient throttle — the common case, since `posts/all` alone is limited to one call per five minutes and back-to-back runs trip it — permanently degrades the run by up to 16x. The tool appears hung rather than slow: the progress bar advances every 48 seconds with no indication that a widened interval, not the network, is the cause.</impact>
<parameter name="fix">Narrow the interval again after sustained success, floored at the documented default:

```go
// narrowRateLimit steps the interval back toward defaultRateLimit after a
// request succeeds. Without it a single 429 leaves the widened interval in
// place for the rest of the run, turning a transient throttle into a
// permanent slowdown.
func narrowRateLimit() {
	rateLimiterMux.Lock()
	defer rateLimiterMux.Unlock()

	if rateLimitInterval <= defaultRateLimit {
		return
	}

	rateLimitInterval /= 2
	if rateLimitInterval < defaultRateLimit {
		rateLimitInterval = defaultRateLimit
	}
	rateLimiter.Reset(rateLimitInterval)
}
```

Call it from `pinboardGet` on the success path, immediately before returning the response. Halving on success rather than resetting outright keeps the client conservative if Pinboard is still near its limit.

Also cap the widening so a pathological run cannot reach an absurd interval:

```go
const maxRateLimit = 60 * time.Second
```

clamped inside `widenRateLimit`.

Test both directions: extend `TestPinboardGet_BacksOffOn429` with an assertion that a following successful call narrows the interval, and add a case asserting the clamp holds at `maxRateLimit`.</fix>
</invoke>

## Evidence

## Impact

## Fix

## Resolution
Added narrowRateLimit, called by pinboardGet on every non-429 response: it halves the interval back toward defaultRateLimit and floors there, so a transient throttle no longer costs the rest of the run. widenRateLimit now clamps at the new maxRateLimit (60s) instead of doubling without bound. Covered by TestRateLimit_WidensOn429AndNarrowsOnSuccess, which drives widen/narrow at production scale (a millisecond fixture sits below the floor and cannot move), and TestWidenRateLimit_ClampsAtMax.
title: The rate-limit interval never recovers, so one transient 429 slows the rest of the run permanently

`run` holds the whole orchestration and the exit-code decision, and no test calls it. Three behaviours filed as findings in the previous audit round are therefore asserted nowhere:

- any rejected write returns 1 via `stats.ApplyErrorCount()` (`audit-796c7609`);

```
main.go:161:  main              0.0%
main.go:217:  setHTTPTimeout    0.0%
main.go:226:  run               0.0%
main.go:268:  closeBody        50.0%
```

The function is straightforwardly testable: it takes `(apiToken string, workers int, dryRun bool)` and reaches Pinboard only through `pinboardAPIEndpoint`, which `useEndpoint` already redirects. `ciMode` suppresses the statistics block, and the helpers to set it exist.

Because the previous regression here was invisible for the life of the tool, the absence of a test is the specific condition that let it persist.</impact>

```go
// A fetch failure must exit non-zero; returning from main exited 0 and let a
// broken scheduled run report success.
func TestRun_FetchFailureExitsNonZero(t *testing.T) {
	resetStats(t)
	setCIMode(t, true)
	server := staticServer(t, http.StatusUnauthorized, "")
	useEndpoint(t, server.URL)

	if code := run(testToken, 1, false); code != 1 {
		t.Errorf("run() = %d, want 1 on a failed fetch", code)
	}
}
```

plus `TestRun_CleanPassExitsZero` (server returns `[]`, expect 0) and `TestRun_RejectedWriteExitsNonZero` (server returns bookmarks then `{"result_code":"something went wrong"}`, expect 1 and `ApplyErrorCount() == 1`).

Add `TestSetHTTPTimeout` asserting both `httpClient.Timeout` and `redirectClient.Timeout` change, restoring them via `t.Cleanup` — the second assignment is easy to drop in a refactor and nothing would notice.

Cover the failure halves of `closeBody` and `reportApplyError` with a `body` whose `Close` returns an error and a `verbose = true` call respectively; both are small and make the stderr routing assertable.

`main` itself calls `os.Exit` and is not worth testing directly — its logic already lives in `validateFlags` and `run`, both of which are testable. Note that in the run summary rather than leaving it as an unexplained 0%.</fix>
</invoke>

## Problem

Every test that touches package state repeats the same three lines: capture the old value, assign the new one, restore in cleanup. Four of the twelve sites skip the helper entirely and inline `t.Cleanup` at the call site, and those four are the ones that can silently leak state if an early `t.Fatal` is added above the cleanup registration.

The pattern is identical in every case and differs only in the variable's type, which Go generics can express directly.</problem>
<parameter name="evidence">Twelve sites, from `grep -n 'previous :=\|old[A-Z][a-zA-Z]* :=' *_test.go`:

```
apply_functions_test.go:247  oldCI := ciMode
apply_functions_test.go:270  oldCI := ciMode
apply_functions_test.go:314  oldCI := ciMode
main_functions_test.go:941   oldCI := ciMode
main_test.go:48              previous := stats
main_test.go:58              previous := pinboardAPIEndpoint
main_test.go:69              oldTitles, oldTags := skipTitles, skipAutoTags
main_test.go:79              previous := verbose
main_test.go:151             previous := unshortenBitly
main_test.go:176             previous := unshortenIsGd
main_test.go:253             previous := isGdEndpoint
main_test.go:310             previous := bitlyEndpoint
```

Five are wrapped in named helpers (`resetStats`, `useEndpoint`, `setSkipFlags`, `setVerbose`, `useBitlyEndpoint`); the other seven are inline, so the four `ciMode` sites each write:

```go
	oldCI := ciMode
	ciMode = false

	t.Cleanup(func() { ciMode = oldCI })
```

There is no `setCIMode` helper, which is also why `TestRun` (filed separately as a coverage gap) has no ready way to suppress the statistics block.

The `isGdEndpoint` site at main_test.go:253 is inside a subtest loop, which is exactly where an early return would skip the restore — and a missed restore here is what produced the data race the race detector caught during the previous round's test rewrite.</evidence>
<parameter name="impact">Seven inline copies mean the correct ordering — capture, assign, register cleanup — is re-derived by hand each time, and one omission leaves package state modified for every test that follows. Because the parallel/serial split in this package already depends on globals being restored promptly, such a leak surfaces as an unrelated test failing later, or as a data race, rather than as a failure in the test that caused it.</impact>
<parameter name="fix">Replace all twelve with one generic helper:

```go
// swap sets *target to value for the duration of the test and restores the
// previous value afterwards. Written once because the capture-assign-restore
// ordering is easy to get subtly wrong, and a missed restore surfaces as an
// unrelated later test failing rather than as a failure here.
func swap[T any](t *testing.T, target *T, value T) {
	t.Helper()

	previous := *target
	*target = value

	t.Cleanup(func() { *target = previous })
}
```

Then:

```go
func resetStats(t *testing.T)                { t.Helper(); swap(t, &stats, newStatistics()) }
func useEndpoint(t *testing.T, url string)   { t.Helper(); swap(t, &pinboardAPIEndpoint, url) }
func useBitlyEndpoint(t *testing.T, u string) { t.Helper(); swap(t, &bitlyEndpoint, u) }
func useIsGdEndpoint(t *testing.T, u string) { t.Helper(); swap(t, &isGdEndpoint, u) }
func setVerbose(t *testing.T, v bool)        { t.Helper(); swap(t, &verbose, v) }
func setCIMode(t *testing.T, v bool)         { t.Helper(); swap(t, &ciMode, v) }

func setSkipFlags(t *testing.T, titles, autoTags bool) {
	t.Helper()
	swap(t, &skipTitles, titles)
	swap(t, &skipAutoTags, autoTags)
}
```

`swap` also works for the function-valued seams — `swap(t, &unshortenBitly, stub)` — because `T` is inferred as the func type.

Convert the four inline `ciMode` sites and the two inline shortener-seam sites to the helpers. The module is on Go 1.26.6, so generics are available without any version concern.</fix>
</invoke>

## Fix

## Resolution
Added the generic swap[T any](t, *T, T) helper and routed every save-restore through it: resetStats, useEndpoint, useBitlyEndpoint, useIsGdEndpoint, setSkipFlags, setVerbose, and a new setCIMode. The four inline ciMode blocks and the two inline shortener-seam blocks now call the helpers, and the isGdEndpoint block inside the subtest loop uses useIsGdEndpoint. grep for the old pattern now matches only swap's own body. setCIMode is also what let the new TestRun cases suppress the statistics block.

## Problem

`url.Values` is a map, so it is passed by reference. `pinboardGet` calls `params.Set("auth_token", apiToken)` on the caller's own value, meaning every caller's local `params` map holds the token after the call returns.

No current caller reads `params` afterwards, so nothing leaks today. The hazard is that the map looks like caller-owned input while silently becoming credential-bearing state.</problem>
<parameter name="evidence">main.go:301-304:

```go
func pinboardGet(path string, params url.Values, apiToken string) (*http.Response, error) {
	params.Set("auth_token", apiToken)
	params.Set("format", "json")
	apiURL := pinboardAPIEndpoint + path + "?" + params.Encode()
```

The largest caller is `updateBookmark` (main.go:710-727), which builds a seven-key map and hands it over:

```go
	params := url.Values{
		paramURL:      {newURL},
		"description": {titleToUse},
		...
	}
	...
	resp, err := pinboardGet(path, params, apiToken)
```

After that call `params["auth_token"]` holds the token. A later diagnostic such as `fmt.Fprintf(os.Stderr, "update params: %v\n", params)` — the obvious thing to add when debugging a rejected write — would print the credential, and would look harmless at the point it is written because the map is visibly local and visibly built from bookmark fields only.

This is the same class as the confirmed transport-error leak filed separately: the token is reachable from a value whose name does not suggest it carries one.</evidence>
<parameter name="impact">No leak today. The risk is a future diagnostic or structured-logging call over what appears to be a request-parameter map, which would print the account credential. Given that two token-disclosure findings have already been confirmed in this codebase, leaving a third latent path is not worth the two lines it costs to close.</impact>
<parameter name="fix">Copy before mutating, so the caller's map is never touched:

```go
func pinboardGet(path string, params url.Values, apiToken string) (*http.Response, error) {
	// Copy rather than mutate: url.Values is a map, so setting auth_token on
	// the caller's value would leave the credential in a map the caller may
	// later log as ordinary request parameters.
	query := make(url.Values, len(params)+2)
	maps.Copy(query, params)
	query.Set("auth_token", apiToken)
	query.Set("format", "json")

	apiURL := pinboardAPIEndpoint + path + "?" + query.Encode()
```

`maps.Copy` is standard library and the module is on Go 1.26.6. The copy is shallow — the `[]string` slices are shared — which is fine here because no caller mutates a value slice after the call.

Add an assertion to an existing update test that `params` does not contain `auth_token` after `updateBookmark` returns, so the property is pinned rather than merely intended.</fix>
</invoke>

## Evidence

## Impact

## Fix

## Resolution
pinboardGet now copies the caller's url.Values with maps.Copy into a local query before setting auth_token and format, so the credential never lands in a caller-owned map. Pinned by TestPinboardGet_DoesNotMutateCallerParams, which asserts the caller's params gained neither auth_token nor format after the call.
title: pinboardGet writes the auth token into the caller's url.Values, leaving a credential in a caller-owned map

## Problem

`fixParenthesesSuffix` only returns the trimmed URL after confirming it answers HTTP 200. `expandAndCheckURL` then treats that return value as a changed URL and calls `validateURLAccessibility` on it, issuing a second HEAD to the URL just proven live.

The same shape does not apply to the other two steps: `expandURL` returns a URL it never probed, and `urlRedirects` returns a *different* URL from the one it probed, so both genuinely need validating.</problem>
<parameter name="evidence">main.go:1009-1025 — the first HEAD, gating the return:

```go
	resp, err := httpClient.Head(updatedURL)
	...
	if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusOK {
		stats.IncrementParenthesesFixed()
		...
		return updatedURL, nil
	}

	return urlString, nil
```

main.go:936-952 — the second HEAD on the same value:

```go
	for _, step := range steps {
		next, err := step.fn(current, verbose)
		...
		if next == current {
			continue
		}
		...
		if err := validateURLAccessibility(next, step.name); err != nil {
			return "", err
		}
```

Because `fixParenthesesSuffix` returns `updatedURL` only on 200, `next != current` implies the URL was just confirmed live, so the follow-up HEAD cannot change the outcome.

The waste is bounded: it costs one extra request per bookmark whose URL ends in `)`, not per bookmark. `stats.RecordHTTPStatus(opURLValidation, ...)` also double-counts those, so the URL Validation totals slightly overstate the number of distinct checks.

This is the residue of the previous round's fix for `audit-467363cc`, which removed three redundant validations in the common path and left this one on the rare path.</evidence>
<parameter name="impact">One extra HEAD per Markdown-mangled bookmark, plus a small over-count in the URL Validation statistics. Negligible on a typical account and not worth a behavioural risk to remove; worth recording so it is not rediscovered as new.</impact>
<parameter name="fix">Two options, in order of preference.

Prefer restructuring so the step reports whether its result is already validated:

```go
type urlStep struct {
	name string
	fn   func(string, bool) (string, error)
	// validated is true when fn only returns a rewritten URL it has already
	// confirmed reachable, so expandAndCheckURL can skip the follow-up HEAD.
	validated bool
}

steps := []urlStep{
	{name: "expanded URL", fn: expandURL},
	{name: "fixed URL", fn: fixParenthesesSuffix, validated: true},
	{name: "redirected URL", fn: urlRedirects},
}
```

with the loop skipping `validateURLAccessibility` when `step.validated` is set. The flag documents the coupling rather than hiding it.

The alternative — having `fixParenthesesSuffix` return the trimmed URL without probing it, and letting `expandAndCheckURL` do the single check — is a smaller diff but changes behaviour: the function currently keeps the original URL when the trimmed one is not exactly 200, whereas `validateURLAccessibility` accepts any non-4xx. That would start rewriting URLs on a 3xx or 5xx answer, so it is not a safe swap.

If neither is taken, leave the finding open rather than closing it silently; the cost is genuinely small.</fix>
</invoke>

## Evidence

## Impact

## Fix

## Resolution
Fixed more thoroughly than the finding proposed. Rather than flagging fixParenthesesSuffix as self-validating, the redirect probe and the liveness check — which were two HEADs of the same URL — were merged into one checkURL that returns both verdicts, with followRedirects walking the chain and checking each hop. urlRedirects was removed; validateURLAccessibility is now a thin wrapper over checkURL for callers that want only the verdict. The common path is one request instead of two, and the parenthesis path two instead of three. Following the chain to a fixed point (bounded by maxRedirectHops = 5) also closes the "resolves only one hop" limitation noted in audit-a6594387's fix text. The ported redirect tests plus TestFollowRedirects_WalksChain, _StopsAtHopLimit, and _ReportsDeadLink cover it.
title: A parenthesis-trimmed URL is HEADed twice: once to test it, once to validate the same result

```
go 1.26.6
```

```markdown
- Go 1.25.6 or later (see `go.mod`)
```

```
go version go1.26.6 linux/amd64
```

```markdown
- Go as specified in [`go.mod`](go.mod) (currently 1.26.6)
```

```markdown
- Go — see the `go` directive in [`go.mod`](go.mod)
```

Either keeps one source of truth. If the parenthetical version is kept, note that Renovate updates `go.mod` automatically, so the README will need the same bump in each such PR.</fix>

## Fix

## Resolution

## Problem

Class: config-drift. The Go version is declared twice: `go = "1.27.2"` in mise.toml and `toolchain go1.27.3` in go.mod. The comment above the pin says it "Must match the `toolchain` line in go.mod", and it does not. mise has a first-class mechanism that reads the version straight from go.mod (`idiomatic_version_file_enable_tools = ["go"]`), but mise.toml turns it off with `idiomatic_version_file_enable_tools = []`. The stated reason is wrong. The comment says reading go.mod is deprecated, but mise's Go docs say mise reads `toolchain goX.Y.Z` as an exact version request. Only a patch-less `go X.Y` directive is deprecated as a source. The same comment also says the `go` directive is 1.25.0; go.mod says `go 1.26.0`.

## Evidence

mise.toml:13-16 `# Must match the toolchain line in go.mod ... (1.25.0, the floor ...)` / `go = "1.27.2"`; mise.toml:37-41 `... Reading it is deprecated anyway ...` / `idiomatic_version_file_enable_tools = []`; go.mod:3 `go 1.26.0`, go.mod:5 `toolchain go1.27.3`.
Observed in this checkout: `which go` resolves to `mise/installs/go/1.27.2`, `go env GOTOOLCHAIN` = `auto`, `go version` = go1.27.3, but `GOTOOLCHAIN=local go version` = go1.27.2. Go's own toolchain switching, not mise, selects the version that actually runs.
`GOTOOLCHAIN=local govulncheck -scan module` → `Vulnerability #1: GO-2026-6809  Found in: stdlib@go1.27.2  Fixed in: stdlib@go1.27.3`. Under go1.27.3: `No vulnerabilities found.`
In a scratch dir holding only go.mod and `idiomatic_version_file_enable_tools = ["go"]`, `mise current go` → `1.27.3` (source: go.mod). mise docs (mise.jdx.dev/lang/go.html, "Version files") say mise reads `toolchain goX.Y.Z` as an exact version request, and reading a `go X.Y` directive without a patch is what is deprecated.
Renovate bumps the two pins in separate PRs (#71 mise go 1.27.1→1.27.2; #78 go.mod toolchain 1.27.2→1.27.3 [security]), so drift recurs with every Go release.

## Impact

The mise pin does not select the version that runs. When go.mod moves ahead, every fresh checkout installs a Go that it immediately abandons for a second download. Anyone running with `GOTOOLCHAIN=local`, `GOTOOLCHAIN=path`, or with no network access to proxy.golang.org builds and tests with the vulnerable go1.27.2 standard library and gets no warning. The comment asserts an invariant that is false, and a false rationale keeps the duplicate pin in place.

## Fix

Delete `go = "1.27.2"` and its comment block from `[tools]`. Replace `idiomatic_version_file_enable_tools = []` with `idiomatic_version_file_enable_tools = ["go"]`, commented to say that Go comes from go.mod's `toolchain` directive, the same line setup-go's `go-version-file` reads. Verify with `mise current go` → 1.27.3 and `GOTOOLCHAIN=local go version` → go1.27.3. Renovate then has one Go pin to bump (gomod depType `toolchain`).

## Resolution
Removed `go` from mise.toml [tools]; idiomatic_version_file_enable_tools = ["go"], so mise reads go.mod's toolchain line. Verified: mise current go → 1.27.3; GOTOOLCHAIN=local go version → go1.27.3.
title: mise pins Go 1.27.2 while go.mod's toolchain is 1.27.3; mise's go.mod reading is disabled on a misread deprecation

## Problem

Class: unpinned tool in a privileged job, a variant of unpinned-action. Each action is pinned by SHA, but the tools they download are not. goreleaser-action takes `version: "~> v2"`, which resolves to the newest v2 release at run time. download-syft gets no `syft-version`, so it installs whatever version that action release defaults to. cosign is pinned (`v2.6.5`), but separately from mise.toml's `cosign = "2.6.5"`. Go comes from setup-go. None of these come from mise.toml, which claims to pin "every tool the repo actually invokes ... so a local run matches CI".

release.yml:20-22 `contents: write` / `id-token: write`; release.yml:36-39 `cosign-installer ... cosign-release: "v2.6.5"`; release.yml:41-42 `anchore/sbom-action/download-syft@66cbf4bc... # v0.24.3` with no `with:`; release.yml:44-48 `goreleaser/goreleaser-action@a4f02ab5... # v7.3.0` / `version: "~> v2"`. A tag pushed today builds with a goreleaser that is less than a day old and has never run locally against this .goreleaser.yml. A compromised or broken goreleaser or syft release executes inside the job that holds a repo write token and the OIDC identity used to sign checksums. A broken minor release fails the release on the tag. The local snapshot does not exercise the CI release toolchain.

release.yml: setup-go, cosign-installer, download-syft and goreleaser-action replaced by jdx/mise-action@8418fedb (v5.2.2, cache: false) plus `mise run release-publish`. goreleaser, cosign and syft come from mise.toml pins and Go from go.mod. actionlint and zizmor --pedantic clean.

## Problem

AUD:S1 Privacy. `just release` is documented as "Run GoReleaser (dry-run by default)" and runs `goreleaser release --clean --skip=publish --snapshot`. Snapshot mode does not skip the `signs` pipe. GoReleaser invokes `cosign sign-blob ... --yes` on checksums.txt. Outside GitHub Actions, keyless cosign has no ambient OIDC token, so it starts an interactive browser login. On success it records a certificate carrying the developer's email in Sigstore's public, append-only Rekor transparency log. `--yes` suppresses cosign's prompt that warns about exactly that. mise.toml:29-31 installs cosign locally so the snapshot runs this stage.

## Evidence

Justfile:34-36 `# Run GoReleaser (dry-run by default)` / `release:` / `goreleaser release --clean --skip=publish --snapshot`. .goreleaser.yml:86-96 `signs: - cmd: cosign ... args: [sign-blob, ..., "--yes"] artifacts: checksum`. Reproduced in a scratch clone with a stub `cosign` on PATH: `goreleaser release --clean --skip=publish,sbom --snapshot` logged `• signing  cmd=cosign artifact=checksums.txt ...`, and the stub recorded `STUB-COSIGN-CALLED: sign-blob --output-certificate=dist/checksums.txt.pem --output-signature=dist/checksums.txt.sig dist/checksums.txt --yes`. mise.toml:29-31 `goreleaser shells out to these during just release: signs.cmd: cosign ...`.

## Impact

A developer who runs the "dry-run" either gets an unexpected browser login, or a headless run fails. If they complete the login, their email address becomes permanently and publicly linked to a throwaway snapshot artifact in Rekor, with no confirmation prompt. The entry cannot be deleted.

## Fix

Skip signing in the local snapshot task: `goreleaser release --clean --skip=publish,sign --snapshot`. Signing stays in the release workflow, where the OIDC identity is the workflow, not a person. Update the mise.toml comment so cosign is described as used by the release workflow, not by the local snapshot.

## Resolution
mise `release` task runs `goreleaser release --clean --snapshot --skip=publish,sign`. Verified with a stub cosign on PATH: `mise run release` exit 0 and zero cosign invocations.
title: The "dry-run" snapshot release runs keyless cosign signing with --yes, publishing the developer's identity to the public Rekor log

## Problem

AUD:S6 Error handling. The marker scan is `grep -rln 'coverage:ignore' ... 2>/dev/null | while ...; done >"$markers"` under `set -euo pipefail`. grep exits 1 when nothing matches, pipefail propagates that, and set -e ends the script before the awk report runs. The redirect `2>/dev/null` also hides any real grep error (exit 2) in the same way. The README invites removing markers ("treat a new one as a claim to verify"), and there is exactly one today, so removing it turns the gate red with no message.

## Evidence

scripts/coverage-gate.sh:27 `set -euo pipefail`; :47 `grep -rln 'coverage:ignore' --include='*.go' . 2>/dev/null |`. `rg -c coverage:ignore --glob '*.go'` → `./main.go:1`. Reproduced in a scratch tree with the script, a fully covered profile, and one .go file without a marker: `bash scripts/coverage-gate.sh coverage.out 100` printed nothing and exited 1. Control, the same tree with one marker: `coverage-gate: 100.0% (1/1 statements)` / `coverage-gate: OK`, exit 0.

## Impact

The gate fails closed but silently: CI goes red on the coverage step with no line saying why. The first person to delete the last unreachable branch will hit it.

## Fix

Make "no match" a normal outcome and keep real errors loud. Replace line 47 with `{ grep -rln 'coverage:ignore' --include='*.go' . || [ $? -eq 1 ]; } |`, which tolerates grep's no-match status 1 and still fails on status 2, and drop `2>/dev/null`. Re-run the zero-marker reproduction and expect `coverage-gate: 100.0%` and exit 0.

## Resolution
coverage-gate.sh: `{ grep ... || [ $? -eq 1 ]; }` replaces `grep ... 2>/dev/null`. Zero-marker reproduction now prints coverage-gate: OK and exits 0; real repo gate 710/710 OK.
title: coverage-gate.sh exits 1 with no output when the tree has no coverage:ignore marker

## Problem

AUD:S20 Commits. Renovate types go.mod `toolchain` bumps as `chore(deps)`, including those marked `[security]`. Those bumps change the standard library compiled into every release binary. The equivalent golang.org/x/net security bumps are typed `fix(deps)`. The type therefore under-reports a user-facing security fix, and the release changelog files it under "Other changes".

## Evidence

git log: e2e4680 `chore(deps): update go toolchain directive (1.27.2 → 1.27.3) [security] (#78)`, diff `go.mod | 2 +-`; 213036c (#68), a1781d6 (#44), 5c76e56 (#39), all `chore(deps): ... toolchain ... [security]`. Compare 037d3cf `fix(deps): update module golang.org/x/net (v0.59.0 → v0.60.0) [security] (#69)`. govulncheck confirms GO-2026-6809 in stdlib@go1.27.2, fixed in 1.27.3, so #78 is a security fix to the binary. The v0.1.0 release notes put `chore(...)` entries under "Other changes". renovate.json only extends `local>ivuorinen/renovate-config`.

## Impact

A user who reads the changelog for security fixes does not see a stdlib vulnerability fix in the release. Commit types are inconsistent between the two kinds of shipped-code dependency.

## Fix

In .github/renovate.json add `"packageRules": [{ "matchManagers": ["gomod"], "matchDepTypes": ["toolchain"], "semanticCommitType": "fix" }]`. Renovate's gomod manager names this depType `toolchain`. Alternatively, set it in the shared ivuorinen/renovate-config so every Go repo gets it.

## Resolution
renovate.json packageRule: matchManagers gomod, matchDepTypes toolchain → semanticCommitType fix. Takes effect on the next Renovate toolchain PR; past commits are immutable.
title: Go toolchain security bumps are committed as chore(deps), understating a fix to the shipped binary

## Problem

Class: cache keyed on the wrong inputs. Go's version now lives only in go.mod, where mise reads it as an idiomatic version file. mise-action's default cache key hashes mise.toml, mise.lock and .tool-versions, not go.mod. When Renovate bumps go.mod's `toolchain` line and mise.toml is unchanged, the primary key is unchanged. The restore is an exact hit on a cache holding the old Go, mise installs the new Go on top, and mise-action skips saving because the key already exists. Every later run repeats the download until mise.toml next changes.

## Evidence

go.yml:31 and :49 `- uses: jdx/mise-action@8418fedb1110381a0d3ba51a7a415d7c1b884550 # v5.2.2`, with no `cache_key`. mise-action src/index.ts@8418fedb:26-52 hash patterns cover `**/mise.toml`, `**/mise.lock`, `**/.tool-versions` and the `.config/mise` variants, but not go.mod. :57 default key `{{cache_key_prefix}}-{{platform}}...-{{file_hash}}`. src/cache-save.ts: `return restoredKey === primaryKey ? undefined : primaryKey` ("An exact hit already exists and needs no save"). Isolated `mise ls --current` resolves `go 1.27.3` from `~/repo/go.mod`. Renovate bumps go.mod's toolchain on its own (#68, #78).

## Impact

After each Go toolchain release, both go.yml jobs (build and lint) download and unpack a full Go distribution on every run, on every PR and on main, until an unrelated mise.toml change rotates the key. It costs time and bandwidth; the version used is still correct.

## Fix

Add go.mod to the key in both go.yml mise-action steps: `with: { cache_key: "{{default}}-${{ hashFiles('go.mod') }}" }`. mise-action documents `{{default}}` plus a suffix for exactly this case. release.yml keeps `cache: false` and needs no change.

## Resolution
Both go.yml mise-action steps set cache_key "{{default}}-${{ hashFiles('go.mod') }}", so a toolchain bump rotates the key and the new Go is cached once. release.yml keeps cache: false. actionlint 0, zizmor --pedantic no findings.

## Problem

AUD:S12 License / AUD:S6 Error handling. The `LICENCE` fix added one more spelling to an exact-match list but kept the failure mode: a linked module whose license file uses any other name is omitted, with no error. That is how godotenv's notice went missing. The loop has no check that each linked module contributed at least one file, and the match is case-sensitive on Linux, where releases are built.

## Evidence

scripts/gen-notices.sh:41-42 `for f in LICENSE LICENSE.txt LICENSE.md LICENCE LICENCE.txt LICENCE.md COPYING NOTICE; do` / `[ -f "$dir/$f" ] || continue`. There is no fallback after the loop (lines 36-52). Real modules in the local module cache that this list misses: `github.com/kr/pretty@v0.3.1: License` and `github.com/kr/text@v0.2.0: License`, whose only license file is named `License`. Adding either as a dependency yields a release whose THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md omits it, and gen-notices.sh exits 0.

## Impact

Any future dependency with a differently spelled license file is redistributed in every release binary without its notice, and nothing reports it. This is the same compliance defect that was just fixed for godotenv.

## Fix

Replace the fixed list with a case-insensitive match over the module root and fail when a module yields nothing:
`found=0; for file in "$dir"/*; do f=${file##*/}; case $(printf '%s' "$f" | tr '[:lower:]' '[:upper:]') in LICENSE | LICENSE.* | LICENSE-* | LICENCE | LICENCE.* | COPYING | COPYING.* | NOTICE | NOTICE.*) ;; *) continue ;; esac; case $f in *.go) continue ;; esac; [ -f "$file" ] || continue; found=1; { ...heading/cat/fence as today... } >>"$out"; done; [ "$found" -eq 1 ] || { printf 'gen-notices: no license file for %s %s\n' "$path" "$version" >&2; exit 1; }`.
Under pipefail, the subshell's `exit 1` fails the pipeline and the release's before hook. Verify by regenerating (7 modules, unchanged), then by pointing the loop at a stub module dir holding only `License`.

## Resolution
gen-notices.sh matches LICENSE/LICENCE/COPYING/NOTICE (with any extension or `-` suffix) case-insensitively over the module root, skips *.go, and exits 1 naming any module with no match. Verified on a scratch module: no license file → exit 1 "no license file for example.com/nolic" (old script: exit 0, 0 modules); `License` → matched. Repo output unchanged at 7 modules. shellcheck 0.
title: gen-notices.sh still skips a module silently when its license file name is not on a fixed, case-sensitive list

## Problem

Class: unpinned tool in a privileged job, the variant of unpinned-action that ci-b733b125 fixed for goreleaser and syft. The fix moved every tool behind mise.toml, but the installer is not pinned: none of the three `jdx/mise-action` steps sets `version:`, so each run installs whatever mise release is newest. In the release job that binary then executes goreleaser, cosign and syft with the write token and the OIDC signing identity.

## Evidence

release.yml:20-22 `contents: write` / `id-token: write`; release.yml:33-38 `uses: jdx/mise-action@8418fedb… # v5.2.2` with only `cache: false` under `with:`; release.yml:40-43 `run: mise run release-publish` with `GITHUB_TOKEN`. go.yml:33-35 and go.yml:53-55 also omit `version:`. mise-action action.yml at 8418fedb: `version: … If not specified, uses the newest release satisfying minimum_release_age` (default `24h`). mise published v2026.10.12, .13, .14, .15, .17 and .18 between 2026-10-16 and 2026-10-23, so a tag pushed on any day runs a mise that has never run locally or in this repo's CI. With `cache: false`, src/index.ts `useBinCache` returns early, so the release job always downloads the newest release (verified against minisign-signed checksums, which proves authenticity, not that the release works).

## Impact

A broken mise release fails a tag's release, or changes how tools resolve (Go comes from mise's go.mod reading), with no change in the repository. A compromised release that clears the 24h window runs with a token that can create releases and with the identity cosign signs as, so it can publish signed artifacts. Re-running an old tag uses a different mise than the original run.

## Fix

Add `version: 2026.10.1` to the `with:` block of all three mise-action steps (release.yml:35-38, go.yml:34-35, go.yml:54-55). 2026.10.1 is the version the clean isolated `mise install` of this mise.toml was verified with. No custom manager is needed: Renovate's github-actions manager has `jdx/mise-action` in known-actions/github-release-attachments-dynamic.ts and tracks `with: version` as dependency `jdx/mise` (depType `uses-with`). Bumps then arrive as PRs under the shared config's 3-day minimumReleaseAge. Once `version` is set, mise-action ignores `minimum_release_age`.

## Resolution
`version: 2026.10.1` added to all three mise-action steps (release.yml:39, go.yml:37, go.yml:70), with a comment at the first step in each file. Verified: release v2026.10.1 ships the asset mise-action builds the name for (mise-v2026.10.1-linux-x64) plus a minisign-signed SHASUMS256.txt; a clean isolated `mise install` with mise 2026.10.1 installs all 5 tools. Renovate tracks it natively (known-actions jdx/mise-action → jdx/mise). actionlint and zizmor --pedantic clean.
title: mise-action installs an unpinned mise in the release job, which runs goreleaser and cosign with contents: write and id-token: write

## Problem

HEAD's build job used actions/setup-go with its default `cache: true`, which restores GOMODCACHE and GOCACHE keyed on go.sum. The new job installs Go through mise-action, which caches only mise's own directory, so the Go caches are never restored.

## Evidence

HEAD go.yml:25-29 `uses: actions/setup-go@b7ad1dad… # v7` / `go-version-file: go.mod` (cache defaults to true). Current go.yml:33-35 `uses: jdx/mise-action@8418fedb…` with `cache_key` only. mise-action src/index.ts:445-447 `restoreMiseCache` caches `miseDir()` and nothing else (saveCache, line 1619-1621, the same). Under a clean mise, `go env` gives GOCACHE `~/.cache/go-build` and GOMODCACHE `~/go/pkg/mod`, both outside the mise directory. Measured with empty caches on 8 cores, using the same Go 1.27.3: `go build` 11.5s cold vs 0.4s warm, `go test -race` 21.0s cold vs 1.8s warm. The caches it would restore are 239 MB (build) and 32 MB (modules).

## Impact

About 30s more per build-job run on 8 cores, and more on a 4-vCPU hosted runner, on every PR push and every push to main. There is no correctness impact.

## Fix

In the build job, add one step right after mise-action: `- uses: actions/cache@55cc8345863c7cc4c66a329aec7e433d2d1c52a9 # v6.1.0` with `path: |` listing `~/.cache/go-build` and `~/go/pkg/mod`, `key: go-${{ runner.os }}-${{ hashFiles('go.mod', 'go.sum') }}` and `restore-keys: go-${{ runner.os }}-`. Comment it: mise-action caches only mise's directory. Leave the release job uncached, as it is now.

## Resolution
go.yml:40-50: actions/cache@55cc8345… # v6.1.0 (the v6.1.0 tag's commit) after mise-action in the build job, using the paths actions/cache documents for Go on Linux (~/.cache/go-build, ~/go/pkg/mod). The key adds go.mod to the documented go.sum hash, so a toolchain bump gets a new key instead of an exact hit that is never re-saved. Paths match `go env GOCACHE GOMODCACHE` under a clean mise. actionlint and zizmor --pedantic clean. Not run on GitHub Actions.
title: Moving from setup-go to mise-action dropped the Go module and build cache; every CI build compiles the race-instrumented stdlib from scratch

body:
## Problem

isRedirectStatus puts 302, 303 and 307 in the same set as 301 and 308, and followRedirects returns the last URL it reached as the bookmark's new address. RFC 9110 §15.4.3/§15.4.8 say the opposite for 302/307: the target "resides temporarily under a different URI … the client ought to continue to use the target URI for future requests." For 303, §15.4.4, the target is a different resource. An anonymous HEAD to any page behind a login receives exactly such a temporary redirect to the login form. The tool rewrites the bookmark to the login URL, and applyUpdateWrite deletes the original entry.

## Evidence

main.go:1394-1398: `case http.StatusMovedPermanently, http.StatusFound, http.StatusSeeOther, http.StatusTemporaryRedirect, http.StatusPermanentRedirect: return true`. main.go:1308 `current = redirect` and main.go:1313 `return current, nil` record no distinction. Observed 2026-10-26: `curl -sI https://github.com/notifications` → `HTTP/2 302`, `location: https://github.com/login?return_to=...`, and likewise for /settings/profile. Reproduced in a scratch copy with a server that 302s every path to /login: `expandAndCheckURL` returned `.../login` for both `/private/doc-1` and `/private/doc-2`, err nil.

## Impact

Every bookmark to a page that needs a session is replaced by a login URL, and the real URL is deleted from Pinboard. That covers SaaS dashboards, intranet pages, settings pages, paywalled articles, and docs shared within an organization. Where the login URL carries no return_to, every such bookmark on that host converges on one address. applyUpdateWrite then posts them all onto that address with replace=yes (see audit-cf9703c9), so N bookmarks collapse into one login-page bookmark. Locale and geo redirects (302 to /en-us/) and cookie-check bounces are rewritten the same way. A user cannot see any of this in the report: it counts as "Redirects followed" and "URLs changed".

## Fix

Persist only permanent hops. In followRedirects keep two values: `current`, the URL being probed, which still walks the whole chain so the liveness verdict comes from the final answer; and `rewrite`, which advances to `redirect` only while every hop so far was 301 or 308. Return `rewrite`. checkURL needs to report whether the redirect was permanent, e.g. return the status alongside the target, or add `isPermanentRedirect(status) bool` covering 301 and 308. Update README.md:167 ("Follows the redirect chain to its final destination") to "Follows permanent redirects (301/308) to their destination; temporary ones (302/303/307) are checked but not written back". Add a test with a 302-to-/login server asserting the bookmark URL is unchanged and the action is ActionNoChange, and one with 301 → 302 → 200 asserting the rewrite stops at the 301 target.

## Resolution
checkURL now also returns whether the hop was permanent (isPermanentRedirect: 301/308 per RFC 9110 §15.4). followRedirects still walks the whole chain for the liveness verdict but advances the written-back URL only while every hop so far was permanent; temporary hops are narrated as 'Temporary redirect followed, URL kept'. README 'How It Works' and the summary line updated. Tests: TestCheckURL_Redirects (permanent column), TestFollowRedirects_KeepsURLBehindTemporaryRedirect (302/303/307), _RewriteStopsAtFirstTemporaryHop, _DeadLinkBehindTemporaryRedirect.
title: Temporary redirects (302/303/307) are written back as the bookmark's new URL, so every login-walled bookmark is rewritten to the login page and the original deleted

body:
## Problem

isDeadLinkStatus rests on the premise that 404 and 410 "assert the resource itself is gone". That does not hold on GitHub. GitHub deliberately answers an unauthenticated request for a private resource with 404 instead of 403, so as not to confirm that it exists. Every check this tool makes is unauthenticated. A bookmark to a private repository, issue, pull request, file or wiki page the user can open in their own browser therefore gets a 404 at checkURL, becomes errDeadLink, and is deleted by applyDeleteAction.

## Evidence

main.go:1388-1389: `return status == http.StatusNotFound || status == http.StatusGone`. main.go:1358-1359: `if isDeadLinkStatus(status) { return "", fmt.Errorf("%w: ...", errDeadLink, ...) }`. main.go:675-679 routes errDeadLink to ActionDelete. GitHub's own documentation (docs.github.com/en/rest/using-the-rest-api/troubleshooting-the-rest-api, "404 Not Found for an existing resource"): "If you make a request to access a private resource and your request isn't properly authenticated, you will receive a 404 Not Found response. GitHub uses a 404 Not Found response instead of a 403 Forbidden response to avoid confirming the existence of private repositories." github.com's web pages apply the same policy to logged-out visitors. README.md:18-19 promises deletion "only on 404 or 410 — the two answers that report the resource itself gone".

## Impact

Irreversible loss of valid bookmarks on the most common host in a developer's Pinboard account. The run reports them as ordinary "Deletions", and nothing in the output distinguishes a private repo from a deleted one. That is the same class of defect as the fixed audit-5fb7b09f ("Every 4xx deletes the bookmark"): a status that describes access, not existence, triggers deletion.

## Fix

Treat a 404 from a host with a documented 404-for-private policy as unverifiable rather than dead. Add `var notFoundMasksPrivate = map[string]bool{"github.com": true, "gist.github.com": true}` with a comment quoting GitHub's doc. In checkURL, before the isDeadLinkStatus branch, return errUnverifiable when `status == http.StatusNotFound && notFoundMasksPrivate[strings.ToLower(resp.Request.URL.Hostname())]`. resp.Request is the request that produced this response, so a redirect into github.com is covered too. Add a test with a 404 response whose Request.URL host is github.com, asserting errUnverifiable and RecordSkipped. Add a sentence to README.md's "Dead Link Detection" and "Error Handling" sections naming the exception.

## Resolution
checkURL returns errUnverifiable for a 404 from a host in checker.notFoundMasksPrivate (github.com, with GitHub's documented policy quoted in the field docstring). gist.github.com deliberately excluded: a secret gist opens by URL, so its 404 does mean gone (deviation from the finding's suggested list). README Dead Link Detection and Error Handling name the exception. Tests: TestCheckURL_NotFoundFromMaskingHostIsUnverifiable (skipped, counted, not deleted), TestNotFoundMasksPrivate_NamesGitHub.
title: Bookmarks of private GitHub repositories, issues and pull requests are deleted: GitHub answers unauthenticated requests for private resources with 404, which the tool treats as "gone"

body:
## Problem

fixParenthesesSuffix trims a trailing ")" from any URL that ends with one, and keeps the trimmed form if the trimmed URL answers HEAD 200. It never checks whether the original URL already worked, and it never checks whether the ")" closes a "(" earlier in the URL. A legitimate URL such as `/wiki/Mercury_(planet)` or a search URL `?q=f(x)` is rewritten whenever the host answers 200 for the truncated path. SPAs with a catch-all route, soft-404 sites, and search endpoints all do. README.md:166 promises the fix applies "when the URL works without it", but what the original URL needs is to not work *with* the paren, and that is never checked.

## Evidence

main.go:1421-1425: `if !strings.HasSuffix(urlString, ")") { return urlString, nil }` then `updatedURL := strings.TrimSuffix(urlString, ")")`. The only acceptance test is main.go:1440 `if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusOK {`, made against the trimmed URL. Reproduced in a scratch copy with a server answering 200 for every path: `expandAndCheckURL(srv.URL+"/wiki/Mercury_(planet)")` returned `.../wiki/Mercury_(planet` with a nil error. Every existing test (main_functions_test.go:411, run_test.go:336, report_test.go:338) uses `/page)`, a URL with unbalanced parentheses, so the balanced case is untested.

## Impact

A working bookmark is rewritten to a broken URL. applyUpdateWrite then posts the broken URL and deletes the original (main.go:866-884), so the correct address is gone from the account. The report counts it as "Parentheses fixed", and nothing marks it as a corruption.

## Fix

Only trim a ")" that has no matching "(". At the top of fixParenthesesSuffix, after the HasSuffix check, add `if strings.Count(urlString, "(") >= strings.Count(urlString, ")") { return urlString, nil }`. This is the balanced-paren rule autolinkers use. It costs no extra request, and Markdown-copied URLs such as `https://x/page)` still get repaired. Add a test with a catch-all 200 server that asserts `fixParenthesesSuffix(srv.URL+"/wiki/Mercury_(planet)", false)` returns its input and issues no request. Change README.md:166 to "Fixes an unbalanced trailing parenthesis when the URL works without it".

## Resolution
fixParenthesesSuffix returns early unless the trailing ')' is unbalanced (count of '(' < count of ')'), issuing no request for balanced URLs. It also no longer returns an error it could never produce. README states the unbalanced rule. Test: TestFixParenthesesSuffix_KeepsBalancedParentheses (catch-all 200 server, /wiki/Mercury_(planet) and ?q=f(x) unchanged, zero requests); existing /page) repair tests unchanged and passing.
title: fixParenthesesSuffix strips the ")" from a live URL with balanced parentheses whenever the host also answers 200 without it

body:
## Problem

RoundTrip runs concurrently, since net/http calls it from every worker. Yet it initializes the struct field on first use with `if t.ua == "" { t.ua = ... }`. httpClient's transport happens to be warmed by getBookmarks on the main goroutine before any worker starts. redirectClient has its own transport instance (main.go:136), and nothing touches it before the pool starts. The first checkURL and unshortenTinyURL calls from up to -workers goroutines therefore read and write t.ua at the same time.

## Evidence

main.go:163-166: `if t.ua == "" { t.ua = "pinboard-checker/" + versionString() + ...`. Reproduced in a scratch copy: eight goroutines issuing Get through one fresh `&http.Client{Transport: newUserAgentTransport()}` under `go test -race` produced `WARNING: DATA RACE  Write at ... (*userAgentTransport).RoundTrip() main.go:164 ... Previous read ... main.go:163`, plus a second race at main.go:173. The suite misses it because safety_test.go:364 and :398 exercise the transport from one goroutine, and by the time any parallel test runs, redirectClient's ua has already been set by an earlier sequential test.

## Impact

A data race on a string header is undefined behaviour under the Go memory model. A torn read can send a garbage User-Agent or fault, and it sits on every production run's first batch of URL checks. CI's `-race` gate, which the workflow describes as "not optional", cannot catch it because the triggering order does not occur in the suite.

## Fix

Drop the lazy field and compute the value once: `var userAgent = sync.OnceValue(func() string { return "pinboard-checker/" + versionString() + " (+https://github.com/ivuorinen/pinboard-checker)" })`. Remove `ua` from userAgentTransport and use `userAgent()` in RoundTrip. Add a regression test that fans eight goroutines through one fresh transport, as the reproduction does, so `-race` fails if the lazy write returns.

## Resolution
The lazily written userAgentTransport.ua field is gone; the User-Agent is a package-level sync.OnceValue read by RoundTrip. Test: TestUserAgentTransport_ConcurrentFirstUse fans 8 goroutines through one fresh transport and asserts all carry userAgent(); the suite passes 3x under -race.
title: userAgentTransport.RoundTrip lazily writes t.ua with no synchronization; the worker pool's first concurrent use of redirectClient is a data race the race detector reports

body:
## Problem

The only irreversible operations this tool performs are posts/delete in applyDeleteAction and mergeIntoExisting, and the delete half of a URL rewrite in applyUpdateWrite. Each reports the affected URL only under -verbose. Without -verbose, a normal run prints counts in the summary but never which bookmarks went. Under -ci, the documented mode for scheduled runs, run() skips stats.Print entirely and prints only the failure count. Pinboard has no trash or undo, so a deleted bookmark's URL, notes and tags exist nowhere once the run ends.

## Evidence

main.go:951-953: `if verbose { fmt.Printf("Deleted: %s\n", action.Original.URL) }`. main.go:907-910: the merge message, also gated on verbose. main.go:460-463: `if !ciMode { fmt.Println(); stats.Print() }`. main.go:467-471 prints only `"%d change(s) failed to apply"`, and only when that count is non-zero. A -ci run that deletes 200 bookmarks and fails nothing therefore exits 0 with empty stdout and stderr.

## Impact

Any wrongful deletion is undetectable and unrecoverable after the fact: the private-GitHub 404s (audit-6b3d40b6), the login-redirect rewrites (audit-cab2c599) and the paren trims (audit-52c6b4c7). The user cannot learn what was lost, let alone restore it, because the notes and tags that made the bookmark worth keeping are discarded with it.

## Fix

Make every destructive write leave a restorable record, whatever the verbosity. Before each posts/delete, write the full original Bookmark as one JSON line (href, description, extended, tags, time, shared, toread) to stderr, prefixed `deleted: `. A user or a script can then replay it through posts/add. Under -ci, also print one count line to stderr at the end ("updated N, deleted M, merged K, skipped S, rejected F"). Add tests asserting the record appears for a non-verbose delete, a merge and a rewrite, and that the -ci count line appears on a run with zero failures.

## Resolution
recordDeletion writes 'deleted (<reason>): <posts/add query>' to the diagnostic stream at every verbosity after each successful posts/delete (dead link, merge, move). The query comes from addParams, now shared with updateBookmark, so it is exactly the call that recreates the bookmark. The record is written after the delete succeeds rather than before, so a rejected delete leaves no false record. -ci prints Statistics.CISummary (updated/deleted/merged/skipped/rejected) to stderr. README 'Deletion records' section warns that the line carries private fields. Tests: TestDeletionsLeaveARestorableRecord (3 paths, all fields), TestFailedDeletionLeavesNoRecord, TestRun_CIModePrintsCountLine.
title: Deletions and URL rewrites leave no record unless -verbose is set, and -ci suppresses even the counts, so an unattended run can delete bookmarks with no trace

body:
## Problem

Four places say that without BITLY_ACCESS_TOKEN a bit.ly bookmark is left exactly as it is. The code does not do that. expandURL swallows errNoBitlyToken and returns the short URL unchanged (main.go:1475-1481). expandAndCheckURL then hands it to followRedirects (main.go:1276), which HEADs it. bit.ly answers HEAD with a 301 to the destination, so the bookmark is rewritten to the destination like any other redirect. If the destination answers 404 or 410, checkURL returns errDeadLink and the bit.ly bookmark is deleted.

## Evidence

README.md:16-17: "bit.ly when `BITLY_ACCESS_TOKEN` is set. An unexpandable short link is left as-is, never deleted". README.md:66-67: "without it, bit.ly links are left unexpanded (never deleted)". .env.example:4-5: "without this bit.ly bookmarks are left unexpanded (never deleted)". main.go:32-34: "bit.ly URLs cannot be expanded without one; they are left untouched rather than treated as broken". Observed 2026-10-26: `curl -sI https://bit.ly/github` → `HTTP/2 301` with a `location:` header, and is.gd answers the same way. main.go:1394-1401 treats 301 as a redirect to follow, and main.go:1358-1359 turns a 404 at any hop into errDeadLink.

## Impact

A user who leaves the token unset, trusting "never deleted", still has bit.ly bookmarks rewritten and, for dead destinations, permanently deleted. The safety statement the user relies on before an unattended run is false.

## Fix

State what happens: "Short links are followed like any other redirect. With BITLY_ACCESS_TOKEN set, bit.ly links are resolved through Bitly's API instead, which avoids Bitly's interstitial pages. A short link whose destination is gone (404/410) is deleted like any other dead link." Apply this to README.md:16-17, README.md:66-67, .env.example:4-5 and the bitlyTokenName comment at main.go:32-34. ## Problem

Every part of a run's state is a package variable, and functions read them implicitly: mode flags (verbose, ciMode, skipTitles, skipAutoTags), the stats singleton, knownURLs, the three endpoints, perHostInterval, the rate limiter, and the swappable collaborators (isPublicHost, repairSteps, the unshorten* vars, readBuildInfo, osExit). Output goes to os.Stdout and os.Stderr directly. cli accepts `stderr io.Writer` but only hands it to the FlagSet; validateFlags, run, closeBody, recordSkip and every verbose message write os.Stderr regardless. The paralleltest linter is enabled in .golangci.yml:62 and then suppressed per test because of this.

## Evidence

`rg -o 'nolint:paralleltest.*'` counts 123 suppressions, with reasons such as "writes to the stats singleton" (22), "repoints pinboardAPIEndpoint" (12), "mutates the skip flags and the stats singleton" (12), and "Cannot run in parallel - modifies global os.Stdout" (8). main.go:321 `func cli(args []string, stderr io.Writer) int` vs main.go:396 `fmt.Fprintf(os.Stderr, "Error: API token is required ...")`. cli_test.go:93 passes io.Discard, yet that error still reaches the real stderr. report_test.go:28 captures output by replacing the process-wide `os.Stderr = write`.

## Impact

Two thirds of the suite cannot run in parallel, so it never exercises the concurrent interleavings the worker pool produces. That is how the redirectClient data race (audit-6155faec) passes a green `-race` run. Every new test must remember the right swap/restore helpers, or it leaks state into the next test. A caller of cli cannot capture its diagnostics. The linter enabled to enforce parallel tests is disabled one test at a time.

## Fix

Introduce one value holding a run's configuration and collaborators, e.g. `type checker struct { out, errOut io.Writer; verbose, ciMode, skipTitles, skipAutoTags, dryRun bool; stats *Statistics; knownURLs map[string]bool; pinboardEndpoint string; client, redirectClient *http.Client; isPublicHost func(string) bool }`. Build it in cli from the parsed flags and the stderr argument. Turn processBookmark, applyBookmarkActions and their helpers into methods. Tests then construct their own checker, call t.Parallel(), and drop the swap helpers, the os.Stdout/os.Stderr capture functions and the 123 nolint comments. If that is too large for one change, first thread cli's `stderr` through validateFlags and run, so the parameter means what its signature says.

## Resolution
All run state moved onto a checker struct: out/errOut writers, mode flags, endpoint, both clients (rebuilt by setHTTPTimeout), isPublicHost, notFoundMasksPrivate, rateLimiter, hostThrottle, stats, knownURLs. The pipeline functions are methods; cli(args, stdout, stderr) splits into configure + run, and every diagnostic reaches the writer cli was given. Statistics.Print takes an io.Writer. Tests build their own checker via newTestChecker with lockedBuffer streams; swap/resetStats/useEndpoint/set* and both os.Stdout/os.Stderr capture helpers are deleted. nolint:paralleltest went from 123 to 7, each naming process-level state: os.Args/osExit, version, readBuildInfo, the pinboardAPIEndpoint seam, t.Chdir, t.Setenv. Suite passes 3x under -race at 100% coverage.
title: All run state lives in package-level globals: 123 tests suppress paralleltest to swap them, and cli's stderr parameter is ignored after flag parsing
